..
Issued at 237 AM EDT Fri Sep 4 2026

PATTERN SYNOPSIS/FORECAST:

Broad upper low over the PacNW with PV max swirling northward 
through Alberta...and a flat but negatively tilted trough axis 
stretching from here to MN/WI at 4z...along/ahead of which 
convection continues to fire. Bulk of the moisture across the CONUS 
remains across the eastern US, particularly from the Gulf Coast up 
into the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes (pwat of 1.56 in on our 0z 
sounding). Some weaker stability just upstream from us over the 
Upper Midwest, aiding in upstream convective activity on the nose of 
a 30kt LLJ stretching from the Plains into MN/WI...interacting with 
that baroclinic zone still stretched out over the region; currently 
have a couple low-level theta-e gradients to contend with...one 
stretching from central WI into southern MI, where convection is 
currently blowing up over SE WI where Tds are in the low-mid 70s 
(this one is associated with the surface stationary boundary 
stretching from MN to MKE through central MI and toward Port Huron; 
and another stretching from the tip of MN into the M-72 corridor 
here in northern MI (Tds south in the 60s, north of this, in the 
50s). Notice some northward propagating lines of convection attm and 
suspect these are likely related to gravity waves. 

Expect ongoing convection to continue to track across the area early 
this morning; think the bulk of the activity will track across the 
area especially after 12z, with the worst conditions across the 
southern half of the area, though think the EUP will not go 
untouched today, especially this morning. Boundary/deformation axis 
to remain in the area through the day into the overnight hours, with 
potential for rain/storms to remain in the region into Saturday 
morning...with improvements likely through the day as we start to 
tap into some drier air and increasing subsidence. High pressure 
should be in control of our weather for Sunday, with return flow 
strengthening across the Plains/MS Valley Monday into Monday 
night...as next system marches into central Canada. Attm, the 
pressure gradient between this and Hudson Bay high looks to increase 
over the Canadian Prairies and perhaps parts of the Upper Midwest, 
and think we could be looking at some slightly stronger flow going 
into the middle of next week...along with potential for more 
showers/storms, perhaps into the latter half of next week, though 
there is increasing uncertainty in the evolution of the system 
marching across southern Canada. 

FORECAST DETAILS...

Heavy rain/storm concerns today...still looking at pwats at or above 
1.5-2in in the region today with that boundary/deformation axis 
present, and worry that some area will get a swath of 1-3in again, 
particularly if any training develops. Have concerns this could 
again impact areas south of M-72, which saw at least an inch of rain 
yesterday (parts of Manistee county, closer to 3-4in), and this 
would heighten flash flooding concerns. (Appears the Manistee River 
basin is running at climatologically high flows for this time of 
year...and all the gauges are upstream of the heaviest swath of rain 
from yesterday.) Deep layer shear remains in play today, and could 
be somewhat perpendicular to the boundary, suggesting there is a 
chance for some feistier storms at times, particularly toward NW 
Lower MI (again) but especially points south and west, where there 
is a better chance at staying a little more unstable than up here. 
(Not to mention we still expect easterly low-level flow to enhance 
low-level shear/spin.) Still have some concerns for water level 
fluctuations in the St. Mary's River system, although the current 
convective complexes aren't moving terribly fast (and pressure 
perturbations seem to be more notable towards Lake MI attm with the 
convection over WI)...but will keep an eye on this, too. 

Still gotta wonder about storms (or at least rain) hanging on 
tonight into Saturday morning; deformation axis with some broad 
low/mid-level forcing and plume of low-level moisture remain in 
place across the region, with at least a few hundred joules of 
instability in play, especially during the morning hours; cooler air 
sneaking in in the lower levels should support a cap developing 
aloft through the day, which should further limit instability (save 
for perhaps a bit of diurnal instability to the inversion and 
perhaps stratocu). Deep layer shear does remain around 25-35kts in 
the region into Saturday morning, too, but may not be collocated 
well with the best instability. Temps aloft Saturday look to fall 
back below 12C and could therefore support a tiny bit of overlake 
instability/shower activity, though on NE flow.
